title: Can good management keep primary health centers open in crises?

When Crises Hit, Can Good Management Keep Primary Health Centers Running?

In low- and middle-income countries, primary health centers (PHCs) are often people's first point of contact with the health system. They provide everything from treatment for common illnesses to chronic disease care, immunization, family planning, and maternal and child health services. When a pandemic hits or health workers strike, some facilities stay open and others close. For the communities they serve, that can mean the difference between getting care and going without. A World Bank Policy Research Working Paper asks whether better management helps public and private PHCs keep services running during major disruptions.

How the Question Was Studied
The study adapted the World Management Survey for use in a low-resource health care setting. The survey measures structured management practices on a scale from 1 to 5, covering areas such as patient flow, inventory management, use of standardized protocols, performance tracking, review of goals, and staff management. In 2021, 429 PHCs and 73 hospitals across Kenya were surveyed, covering both public and private providers. At around the same time, Kenya faced two major shocks in quick succession—the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020 and a national public health workers' strike between December 2020 and January 2021.
To assess whether management quality affected facility performance during these shocks, the survey data was linked to administrative records from Kenya's Health Management Information System, which tracks monthly outpatient attendance at health facilities. This made it possible to compare how attendance diverged over time—before, during, and after the disruptions—across facilities with different management scores and different ownership types.

What the Research Found

PHC’s adoption of structured management practices is limited in both public and private sectors. Kenya's PHCs averaged a management score of just 1.61, well below comparable benchmarks in India (1.87), Brazil (2.20), and the United States (3.11)—and most were clustered near the bottom of the scale.

Private PHCs were better able to maintain services than public ones during disruptions. Both public and private PHCs experienced attendance declines during the first year of COVID-19. During the public health workers' strike, however, the gap widened: public PHC attendance fell while private PHCs remained comparatively stable, consistent with patients shifting toward private providers when public facilities were disrupted.

Within the private sector, better-managed PHCs maintained services more effectively. A one standard deviation increase in management score was associated with 6.5 percentage points higher outpatient attendance during disruptions, relative to the period before. The practices that mattered most were operational ones—managing patient flow, tracking supplies, following protocols, and using data to spot problems early. These systems help managers respond before disruptions translate into missed care. People-management practices, such as hiring, performance evaluation, and staff incentives, were less strongly associated with attendance differences during crises.

In public PHCs, better management did not translate into the same ability to maintain services. This does not mean management is irrelevant in the public sector. It suggests that management practices may be less useful when managers lack the autonomy, tools, or resources to act on them when crises hit.

Figure 2. During disruptions, better management is associated with higher outpatient attendance in private PHCs—but not in public PHCs

Two-panel chart of quarterly coefficients, 2019 Q2 to 2021 Q4, relative to t minus 1 (2019 Q4). In private primary health care facilities, better management is associated with higher outpatient attendance from 2020 Q3 through 2021 Q1, peaking at about 0.065 in 2021 Q1 during the health workers' strike, with confidence intervals above zero in those quarters. In public facilities, coefficients after the start of COVID-19 stay close to zero, between about minus 0.01 and 0.02, with confidence intervals that include zero.

Three Lessons for Policymakers
1.      Management is not a "soft" issue. In essential service delivery, operations management—tracking supplies, managing patient flow, having data-driven meetings—can determine whether a PHC continues to deliver services when crises hit.
2.      Institutional context matters. Strengthening management in public PHCs needs to consider the institutional context, such as whether managers have real authority, adequate resources, and flexibility to respond.
3.      The private sector needs to be part of the strategy. Rather than treating public and private health care as separate, mixed health systems should account for the complementary role private facilities already play during disruptions and consider how to regulate and integrate this role more deliberately.

The Bottom Line
When crises hit, management quality – and specifically the operational systems that keep a facility organized and responsive – can help PHCs continue to provide services.
Private PHCs can absorb patients when public systems are unable to do so, and so health planners can no longer afford to treat the two sectors as unrelated. Building primary health care systems that are able to maintain services during crises means investing in management, reforming institutions, and integrating the private sector—ideally well before the next disruption arrives.
